A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FreeEvent research, with matching authors, task, core method and benchmarks. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval results on SWiG-Event, qualitative comparisons and ablations, and a Real-Event user study in Tables 1–2 and Figures 4–6.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and reports additional evaluation metrics, quantitative ablations, subject-customization comparisons and a hyperparameter case study.

M1.justification: The core two-path FreeEvent procedure and Equations (1)–(6) remain unchanged. Appendix D adds a limited attribute-control adaptation: cross-attention guidance and regulation are applied to attribute words using the masks of their corresponding entities.

E1.justification: Both versions retain SWiG-Event with 5,000 samples and Real-Event with 30 reference images. v2 modestly extends generation requirements through explicit attribute-control tests, including color and material, and subject-customization examples using personalized background concepts. The increased user-study trial count does not establish a new dataset.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds MIGC alongside ControlNet and BoxDiff on SWiG-Event. Appendix E and Figure 9 introduce evaluated comparisons against AnyDoor, PhotoSwap and MS-Diffusion for event-subject customization, substantially broadening the comparison methods. The original six Real-Event baselines remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 expands retrieval evaluation with GSRTR verb-detection accuracy, CLIP-I, DreamSim, DINO, CLIP-T and FID. The user study changes from 30 trials requiring three selections to 50 trials allowing one to three selections. The subject-customization demonstration switches from DreamBooth to Break-A-Scene, and Appendix F introduces a separate experiment with altered guidance and injection schedules.

E4.justification: The original qualitative path and prompt ablations remain. v2 adds quantitative component-removal ablations on Real-Event in Table 3, attribute-control examples in Figure 8, expanded subject-customization investigations, and a shape-mismatch case study comparing guidance and injection schedules in Figure 10. These substantially broaden the analysis of component effectiveness and practical behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Both present point scores and human-judgment counts; the revised number of user-study trials changes evaluation design rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 retrieval values are retained, including FreeEvent's 41.12/63.02/72.74. v2 adds MIGC results and additional metrics, including FreeEvent's 34.10 top-1 verb accuracy and 29.05 FID, plus quantitative ablations and new qualitative outcomes. Table 2 replaces the human-judgment counts under the revised protocol, including FreeEvent's 30 becoming 50; these counts have different trial denominators.

T1.justification: The task definition, diffusion formulation, attention guidance, regulation and feature-injection mathematics in Section 3 are substantively unchanged. No new theorem, proof, derivation or formal assumption is introduced in the appendices.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: single-reference event customization, the training-free FreeEvent framework, compatibility with subject customization, two benchmarks and strong comparative performance. The added experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: Appendix F newly explains how large reference-to-target shape differences create a trade-off between event fidelity and entity appearance, with a tuning remedy. Appendix E qualifies event-subject customization as a secondary capability and acknowledges differing comparison settings. The original limitations concerning small or numerous entities and Stable Diffusion capabilities are retained in Appendix G.

D1.justification: The default implementation settings in Appendix A remain unchanged. v2 additionally documents attribute-to-mask handling and an explicit alternative schedule in Figure 10: guidance increases from 10 to 15 steps, spatial injection decreases from 50 to 30, and self-attention injection decreases from 25 to 15. These are reproducible settings for the added case study, not revised defaults.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new experiments, including MIGC, Break-A-Scene, GSRTR, DreamSim, FID, PhotoSwap and MS-Diffusion, and discusses the relationship to subject-swapping methods. The main related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain largely unchanged. Publication-year and venue updates to existing references do not constitute new cited works.

P1.justification: v2 shortens the abstract, revises the evaluation narrative and expands the appendix organization. Limitations move from the conclusion to Appendix G, the societal-impact paragraph becomes an Impact Statement, and acknowledgements are added. Much of the introduction, related work and method prose remains closely matched, so this is a limited editorial reorganization.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format, with substantially rearranged figures and tables. Figure 3 is repacked, Figure 6 is redesigned, Table 1 gains grouped metric columns, and Table 3 and new analysis figures are added. Qualitative grids are expanded and reorganized, retaining many earlier examples.

improvement.justification: v1's automatic evaluation relied on retrieval, while its component ablations were qualitative. v2 substantially strengthens validation through event-specific verb detection, complementary similarity and quality metrics, MIGC comparisons and numerical component ablations in Table 3. Appendix F also provides concrete guidance about a meaningful failure condition. The subject-customization comparisons remain limited by acknowledged setting differences, and uncertainty reporting is still absent, but the core empirical support and applicability analysis are substantially stronger.
